El mirabrás son alegrías largas (José Menese, con letras de Moreno Galván), y las romeras se atribuyen al Granaíno o a una cantaora llamada la Romera. Hoy el gran intérprete es Chano Lobato.

scenes.name: Los tangos, tientos y marianas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Con bulerías y cantiñas, el gran cante festero: letras de vida, amor y muerte con cierta ligereza, ritmo vivo y pegadizo fácil de seguir con palmas, y un baile sensual. Cádiz y Sevilla se disputan su paternidad, pero los hay en toda Andalucía y en Extremadura; Triana tiene el estilo del Titi y Jerez su propio sello. Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Concert Fatalities Study (1974-2003)
facts.body: A study on concert safety between 1974 and 2003 revealed that 136 people died at rock concerts around the world, with many more sustaining injuries. "136 people died at rock concerts around the world between 1974 and 2003, and many, many, many others have been injured."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Groundbreaking Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
facts.body: The tour supporting the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious and expensive rock had ever seen. It featured elaborate sets, costume changes, choreography, and a cherry-picker boom that took Bowie out over the audience during "Space Oddity." This pushed the basic rock and roll show into unprecedented theatrical territory. "It was hugely expensive and very complex for its day and no one had ever seen anything like it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Cocaine Addiction and Paranoia in Los Angeles (1974-1976)
facts.body: Between 1974 and 1976, Bowie was deeply entrenched in cocaine and alcohol addiction, a state exacerbated by his move to Los Angeles, the "cocaine capital of North America." This led to severe cocaine-induced paranoia, a common reaction among users, with Bowie's focus on witches. "Between 1974 and sometime in 1976, Bowie was an absolute mess."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Obsession with Witches and Bodily Fluids (1974-1976)
facts.body: During his period of intense drug use and paranoia, Bowie became convinced that "witches" were trying to steal his "precious bodily fluids." To prevent this, he began saving all his urine in a fridge and maintained a strict diet of bell peppers and milk to keep his "essence pure," leading his weight to drop below 90 pounds. "Specifically, he got it into his mind that witches, that's as specific as we can get, were out to steal Bowie's precious bodily fluids."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Ambitious Diamond Dogs Tour (1974)
facts.body: The tour accompanying the "Diamond Dogs" album was one of the most ambitious rock had ever seen at the time. It featured elaborate sets, frequent costume changes, complex choreography, and a cherry picker boom that lifted Bowie over the audience during "Space Oddity." This hugely expensive and complex spectacle was groundbreaking, taking the basic rock and roll show to unprecedented levels of theater and spectacle, and audiences loved it. "The tour they came with the Diamond Dogs album was one of the most ambitious things Rock had ever seen."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Unrecorded Eccentricities (1974-1976)
facts.body: The period between 1974 and 1976 saw David Bowie engage in "hundreds" of eccentric and costly endeavors, frequently spending millions on what were considered "truly stupid things." Much of this information remains undocumented in his official biographies because Bowie himself, due to his mental state at the time, could not recall many of these activities or purchases. "quedaron un montón por no decir cientos de estentricidades de David Bogud y esa etapa del 74 a 76 en el cual se gastaba ténticas millonadas en cosas verdaderamente estúpidas."
facts.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

facts.title: Bono's Family Tragedy (1974)
facts.body: On September 10th, 1974, Bono's mother, Iris Hussin, fainted at her father Alex's burial service and suffered a cerebral hemorrhage, dying four days later after being declared brain dead and having life support turned off by Bono's father, Bob. This left Bono, his brother Norman, and his father as "three hardcore Irish bachelor types" suddenly forced to manage on their own. "On September 10th, 1974, Iris Hussin, Bono's mum, gathered the family together and went to the funeral for her father, Bono's grandfather."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stories Behind Songs
facts.name: U2

facts.title: Band Formation (1974)
facts.body: D.D. Ramone and John Cummings decided to form a band in 1974 after getting drunk after work one day. Neither of them knew anything about music at the time, but they were driven by a desire to create it. "That was 1974, and neither guy knew the first thing about music, but they didn't care."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt-Rocks Great Bass Players
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: CBGB Debut (1974)
facts.body: The Ramones began playing at CBGB in New York in 1974, predating the Sex Pistols and The Clash, and two years after Devo formed in Akron, Ohio. "two years before the Ramones started playing CBGB in New York."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Bent Bands
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Debut Performance at CBGB (August 14, 1974)
facts.body: On Wednesday, August 14, 1974, The Ramones played their first-ever show at the iconic New York club CBGB. The initial audience was sparse, consisting of fewer than a dozen people, including the club owner's dog. However, by the end of 1974, the band had performed at CBGB 74 times, with each gig progressively increasing their buzz. The club soon became packed with a diverse crowd, attracting Andy Warhol's circle, intellectuals, wealthy uptown youths seeking to "slum it," and music fans bored with existing sounds and looking for novelty. The Ramones' distinctive style — four "brothers" dressed in torn jeans and leather jackets, playing 1960s-style "bubble gum pop songs" at "a million miles an hour," without solos, stage interaction, or audience acknowledgment, pausing only when Johnny counted off the next song — marked the genesis of the New York punk rock revolution. "The Ramones played their first ever show at a New York club called CBGB."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Formation (1974)
facts.body: The Ramones formed in 1974 when John Cummings (Johnny Ramone) and Douglas Colvin (Dee Dee Ramone) decided to start a band after getting drunk together. They spent $250 on a guitar, bass, and amp, holding their first rehearsal four days later. "They went from beers in a strip club, they got drunk, and they decided that they should form a band."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: CBGB Debut (August 16, 1974)
facts.body: On August 16, 1974, The Ramones played their first gig at CBGB, opening for Television or possibly two other bands. The audience was minimal, with only six people (plus Hilly and his dog) present. They played 20 songs in 17 minutes, characterized by a primitive, ragged, and goofy appearance. "On August 16th, 1974, the Ramones opened for television, or they might have been opening for two other bands. No one really remembers because there were just six people in the bar."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Frequent CBGB Performances (1974-1975)
facts.body: Despite their initial dislike, The Ramones played CBGB 22 more times before the end of 1974, and by early 1975, they began attracting attention and drawing crowds, contributing to CBGB becoming the center of the new music scene. "But with no place else to play, the Ramones returned to CBGB 22 more times before the end of 1974."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 3
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Early Demos and Label Search (1974)
facts.body: The Ramones recorded their first demos in late 1974, costing about $2,000. They sent cassettes and press clippings to every record company they could find, but no one was interested except Sire. "They had recorded their first demos in late 1974, cost them about $2,000."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: First CBGB Show (August 1974)
facts.body: When the Ramones played their inaugural show at CBGB in August 1974, their performance was described as "absolutely terrible." Their distinctive haircuts, leather jackets, and shared last names, combined with their ability to play 15 songs in 20 minutes, led many to question if they were serious or if it was a joke. "When they played their first show at CBGB in August 1974, they were absolutely terrible."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: The four original members connected through a series of introductions: Jeffrey Hyman (Joey) met Douglas Colvin (Dee Dee) at a Sniper show; Douglas introduced Jeffrey to John Cummings (Johnny); and Johnny introduced them to Tommy Erdelyi (Tommy), who already knew Joey from the neighborhood. facts.title: Early Record Claim (1974)
facts.body: Patti Smith's debut 1974 single, featuring an original song (likely "Piss Factory"), is regarded by many music historians as the "first true punk rock record," marking a pivotal moment in the genre's history.

facts.title: Socio-economic Roots (1974)
facts.body: The deconstruction of punk's origins begins in 1974, examining the socio-economic factors that served as a "great musical Big Bang" in history. "Let's start this deconstruction by looking at the socio-economic factors behind one of the great musical Big Bangs in history. And we're going to begin in 1974."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Tina Turner Grammy Nomination (1974)
facts.body: Tina Turner's first solo album, the country record "Tina Turns the Country On!," received a Grammy nomination not in a country category but in an R&B category in 1974. This suggests that despite its country focus, critics perceived a strong R&B or blues influence in her performance. "it did earn her a Grammy nomination but not in a country category but in an R&B category."

facts.title: Confrontation at Michigan Palace (1974)
facts.body: Following a brutal confrontation with a Detroit gang, Iggy Pop performed at Michigan Palace where he provocatively demanded that the gang come on stage and "beat him to a pulp," with some friends believing he sought to die on stage. The audience responded by throwing beer bottles, not all of them empty, at the stage, an incident captured on the album "Metallic KO." "Years later a cassette recording of that performance would be released on an album called Metallic KO."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

He had no money or place to live, and the low point came when the LAPD found him hiding under the counter of a burger joint. facts.title: Confrontation at Michigan Palace (1974)
facts.body: Following a brutal confrontation with a Detroit gang, Iggy Pop performed at Michigan Palace where he provocatively demanded that the gang come on stage and "beat him to a pulp," with some friends believing he sought to die on stage. The audience responded by throwing beer bottles, not all of them empty, at the stage, an incident captured on the album "Metallic KO." "Years later a cassette recording of that performance would be released on an album called Metallic KO."

facts.title: Grammy and CMA Controversy (1974)
facts.body: Olivia Newton-John faced significant criticism from the country music industry when she won a Grammy in 1974 for "Let Me Be There" and was named Female Vocalist of the Year at the CMAs the same year. This led to protests from purists like George Jones and Tammy Wynette, who left the Country Music Association. "She upset a lot of people in the country music industry for winning a Grammy in 1974 for her vocals for Let Me Be There."

facts.title: Win at CMA and Grammy Awards (1974)
facts.body: In 1974, Olivia Newton-John won both the Country Music Association's Female Vocalist of the Year award, beating out Loretta Lynn, Dolly Parton, Tanya Tucker, and Ann Murray, and the Grammy for Female Country Vocalist of the Year, triumphing over Maria Osmond, Barbara Fairchild, Tammy Wynett, and Dottie West. These victories, especially for "I Honestly Love You," caused significant "confusion" and opposition among country music purists who did not consider her music genuinely country. "And you know what? Olivia won them both."

facts.body: Representing Britain in the Eurovision Song Contest, Olivia Newton-John was reportedly forced to sing a song called "Boom Bang" while dressed in a "matronly light blue dress" that resembled a nightgown. She later stated that "no dress could have saved that horrific song," and she faced strong competition from Abba's winning performance of "Waterloo." facts.title: Last Original Show (February 9, 1974)
facts.body: The final show played by The Stooges before their first long hiatus was on February 9, 1974, at The Rock'n'Roll Farm, a biker bar in Wayne, Michigan. Iggy, wearing a pink leotard, provoked the biker audience with insults during a 45-minute rendition of "Louis Louis," leading to eggs and bottles being thrown. Iggy then confronted a large biker, was punched in the face, and the band left the stage, effectively ending their run. "The last show the studios played together was at a club called The Rock'n'Roll Farm in Wayne, Michigan."

facts.title: Origin of Daft Punk's Helmets – 1974 Brian De Palma Film Phantom of the Paradise; Sampler Explosion Fiction September 9, 1999
facts.body: After their rock band Darlin' dissolved in 1992 (following a Melody Maker review calling them "daft punky trash"), Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo shifted to synths, drum machines, and sequencers. One of them saw the 1974 Brian De Palma film Phantom of the Paradise, whose disfigured main character Winslow Leech wore a helmet to hide his injuries — and Daft Punk adopted the helmet idea. The fictional mythology was that at 9:09am on September 9, 1999, a sampler exploded in their studio, horribly injuring both men and requiring helmets to be permanently installed; they had also become robots, losing all human memories but retaining the ability to create music. The helmets had built-in air conditioning (handy for hot live shows) and communication links. One set was made by the same special effects company that worked on one of the Spider-Man movies. Thomas and Guy-Manuel could walk through crowds at their own shows unrecognized. "For us, it was sci-fi glam. We're not performers, we're not models. It would not be enjoyable for humanity to see our features, but the robots are exciting to people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A History of Anonymous Bands
facts.name: Daft Punk

facts.title: The Robot Helmets – 1974 Phantom of the Paradise; Air Conditioning; Communication Links; Spider-Man Effects Company
facts.body: The robot mythology was inspired partly by the 1974 Brian De Palma film Phantom of the Paradise, in which disfigured character Winslow Leech wore a helmet to hide his injuries, and partly by a 1970s band called Space, whose members wore helmets and spacesuits for anonymity. The first helmets had wigs (Thomas had curly hair, Guy-Manuel had long straight hair) until on the way to a 2001 magazine photo shoot they decided robots should look bald and ripped out the fake hair. The helmet designs became increasingly ornate: some reportedly had built-in air conditioning and communication links so they could talk to each other and their crew during performances. One set of helmets was made by the same special effects company that worked on one of the Spider-Man movies. The anonymity was so effective they could walk right through crowds at their own shows unrecognized. One impostor ran up a huge bar tab at a club in Ibiza by claiming to be Thomas Bangalter. "People thought the helmets were marketing or something, but for us, it was sci-fi glam."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Daft Punk

facts.title: Origin of Stage Name "Donna Summer" (1974)
facts.body: Donna Gaines married Austrian actor Helmuth Sommer in Vienna in 1973, taking his surname. Her stage name, "Donna Summer" (S-U-M-M-E-R), was an accidental misspelling by German label Lark Records on her 1974 single "Denver Dream," a spelling that stuck and outlasted her three-year marriage. "when the newly married Donna Sommer recorded a track for German label Lark Records in 1974, the single was pressed and labeled as Donna Sommer, S-U-M-M-E-R. The name with that spelling not only stuck, it outlasted Donna's first marriage."

facts.title: "Sham Corporation" Ruling (1974)
facts.body: A court ruled in 1974 that "Five Platters Inc." was a "sham corporation" whose sole purpose was to illegally deprive band members of their ownership in the band name, and that Book Ram had unfairly benefited from an unbalanced bargaining position. This ruling briefly voided FPI's trademark. "there was a court ruling back in 1974 that the whole purpose of five platters ink had been to illegally deprive the band members of their ownership in the band name, that it was a sham corporation."

facts.title: Disconnected from Mainstream (1974)
facts.body: In 1974, Prog Rock, characterized by its "virtuoso performances," was a big genre but difficult for the average person to connect with. It was seen as part of the "bad shape" music was in, with millionaire rock stars living decadent lives disconnected from ordinary people. "There was Prague Rock with its virtuoso performances, that was a big thing, but it was hard for the average person to identify with that."

facts.title: CD Development and Naming (1974-1979)
facts.body: In 1974, a group of Philips engineers led by Lou Ottens began researching ways to improve vinyl records. They experimented with a 20-centimeter disk before settling on an 11.5-centimeter diameter, a size chosen because it matched the diagonal width of Philips' own compact cassette. In 1979, Philips teamed with Sony to develop the compact disk, contributing expertise in manufacturing processes and proposing the "compact disk" name, leveraging its prior success with the "compact cassette." `"In 1974, a group of engineers within Phillips led by Lou Ottens started to look for ways to improve on the vinyl record."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Potential Proto-Goth/Death Metal Inventor (1974)
facts.body: Paul Williams' work in "Phantom of the Paradise" in 1974, particularly the "Rock Opera" within the film and the fictional band The Undead (whose singer, Peter Ebling, wore corpse paint similar to modern death/black metal), leads to a theory that he accidentally invented proto-goth or proto-death metal music. Goth music didn't widely emerge until bands like Bauhaus in the late 1970s, and death metal in the mid-1980s.

facts.title: Lyrical Content
facts.body: "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" is explicitly about sex, a theme that Randy Bachman later ironically referred to as his "greatest mistake" given his strict rules for band members. "You ain't seen nothing yet. It's clearly about sex."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Randy Bachman's Initial Disbelief
facts.body: Randy Bachman initially did not believe that "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" would become a hit single, having written it as an internal joke and not taking it seriously. "Backman did not think that you ain't seen nothing yet would be that song."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Origin as a Joke
facts.body: Randy Bachman wrote the song as a "not very nice joke" targeting his brother, the BTO II's brother, who had a stutter, incorporating stammering into the vocals. "He wrote it, as I will say, not very nice joke to make BTO2's brother who had a bit of a stutter."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Label Head's Discovery
facts.body: During a review of the "Not Fragile" album, the band played "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" for Charlie Fach, the head of their label, despite Randy Bachman's dismissive attitude toward it. Fach immediately recognized its potential, declaring it "magic" and insisting it be on the album. "So the band plays, you ain't seen nothing yet. Charlie Fatsch took it out and heard it. He was the head of the label and he said, this is magic. I have an earthy thing like this on the radio. You must put it on the album."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Randy Bachman's Reluctance
facts.body: Despite label head Charlie Fach's enthusiasm, Randy Bachman was highly reluctant to include "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" on the album, deeming it "nuts" because the guitars were out of tune, his vocals were stammering and sounded like "bad Van Morrison impressions," and he considered it an unfinished "blurting out lyrics" rather than a proper song. "I said, you're nuts. The guitars aren't even in tune. I'm stammering and doing bad van morse and worse in impressions. I don't know what I'm doing. This isn't even a song. I haven't even written it. I'm just blurting out lyrics."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Fach's Conviction
facts.body: Charlie Fach, the label head, overruled Randy Bachman's objections, calling the raw, unpolished track "charming." He cited his past success discovering Rod Stewart's "Maggie May" (which was seven and a half minutes long and shouldn't have been a single) as proof of his intuition, confidently declaring "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" would be a "career song." "And he said, no, it's charming. I discovered Maggie May for Rod Stewart and that shouldn't have been a single because it was like seven and a half minutes long. Believe me, this would be a career song."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Enduring Success Prophecy
facts.body: Charlie Fach accurately predicted the song's enduring impact, telling Randy Bachman that he would be "singing it every day of your life and you'll be grateful to sing it every day of your life," and that it, along with "Taking Care of Business," would be BTO's "career songs." "He said, you were singing it every day of your life and you'll be grateful to sing it every day of your life. That and taking care of business are going to be your songs."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Inclusion on Album
facts.body: Despite his strong reservations, Randy Bachman "relented" and included "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" on the "Not Fragile" album after the insistence of label head Charlie Fach. "So I relented and put it on the album."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Worldwide #1 Hit
facts.body: Contrary to Randy Bachman's expectations, "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" became a massive international success, reaching number one in 22 countries. "They went to number one in 22 countries."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Million-Selling Single
facts.body: "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" was Bachman-Turner Overdrive's sole million-selling single, a significant commercial achievement that surpassed expectations. "There's BTOs, only single million seller."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: International Covers
facts.body: The song's global popularity led to it being covered in numerous languages, possibly "10 or 12 different languages," including German, Bavarian, and Finnish, and was even adapted into dance disco hits. "And got covered in maybe 10 or 12 different languages. German, Bavarian, Finland, everybody did this song. It's been covered many times as a dance disco hit."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Randy Bachman's Gratitude
facts.body: Randy Bachman expressed eternal gratitude for "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" and "Taking Care of Business," acknowledging that they provided substantial financial benefits over the years, metaphorically buying "a lot of cornflakes for a lot of kids, a lot of gas for my cars." "And I'm eternally grateful to this song. You ain't seen nothing at the taking care of business because it's bought a lot of cornflakes for a lot of kids, a lot of gas for my cars over the years."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Influences
facts.body: According to Tom Bryan, Randy Bachman has openly acknowledged that "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" incorporated several musical influences, including the cowbell from Free's "All Right Now," the beat from The Doobie Brothers' "Listen to the Music," the rhythm guitar from The Who's "Baba O'Riley," and a guitar medley from Dave Mason's "Only You Know and I Know." "Backman is very open about the fact that you ain't seen nothing yet is a song that is kind of pieced together from other influences like the cowbell from all right now by free and the beat from Listen to the Music by the Dubie Brothers. Certainly the rhythm guitar from Bobo O'Reilly by the Who and this guitar medley from only you know and I know."
facts.episode: Ep. 45 - Oh, Canada! Canada's Rock Music Industry in the 70s
facts.name: You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet

facts.title: Chart & Award Success
facts.body: "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet" reached number one on both the Billboard Hot 100 and Canada's RPM chart in the week of November 9, 1974. It later received a Juno Award in 1976 for being the best-selling single in Canada. "Number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and on Canada's counterpart RPM, the week of November 9th, 1974 and it won a Juneau Award for the best selling single in Canada in 1976."

facts.body: This album marked Kraftwerk's first worldwide success and was a pivotal point where the band shed any remaining traces of rock culture. It was highly impactful, notably influencing David Bowie, who played the album in full before his "Station to Station" tour shows. facts.title: Underdog Status for Rumble in the Jungle (1974)
facts.body: At 32 years old, Ali was widely regarded as a significant underdog against the heavyweight champion George Foreman for the Rumble in the Jungle. This perception helped transform him from a controversial figure into a national treasure, with even his corner man, boxing legend Archie Moore, expressing fears that Foreman might kill Ali. "And you would have been hard pressed to find anyone who believed that Muhammad Ali at the age of 32 could beat the heavyweight champion, George Foreman."

facts.title: Mobutu's Favor (1974)
facts.body: For the Rumble in the Jungle, Muhammad Ali received $5 million to fight in Zaire and was flown to the country on President Mobutu's personal plane, highlighting the preferential treatment he received from the Zairian dictator. "They didn't get to fly into Zaire on Mobutu's personal plane the way Ali did."

facts.title: Overloaded Flight to Zaire (1974)
facts.body: Ali's plane journey to Zaire was so heavily laden with James Brown's musical equipment that it "barely made it off the ground," illustrating the significant logistical challenges and the volume of gear transported for the music festival. "Ali crammed onto a plane that was so overloaded with James Brown's gear that the plane barely made it off the ground."

facts.title: Rumble in the Jungle Victory (1974)
facts.body: In the iconic Rumble in the Jungle fight in Zaire, Muhammad Ali knocked out George Foreman in the eighth round, reclaiming the heavyweight championship of the world in 1974. This victory, timed for US television, cemented his comeback as an underdog and further solidified his status as potentially "the most famous black man in the world." "Muhammad Ali knocked out George Foreman in the eighth round and reclaimed the heavyweight championship of the world."
